neurological_exam.gait: Mildly stooped posture. Reduced right arm swing, left arm swing relatively preserved. Stride length mildly shortened. Initiation slightly hesitant. neurological_exam.additional: Resting tremor observed in the right hand at 4-6 Hz with a pill-rolling quality, present while hands resting in the lap and re-emerging during ambulation. There is also a mild action/postural tremor component of approximately 6-8 Hz noted when arms are extended, most prominent in the right hand. No tremor observed at rest in the left hand. Handwriting sample shows progressive micrographia. Glabellar tap sign positive with failure to habituate after 10 taps (Myerson sign).

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive right hand tremor and stiffness with slowing of movements over the past 18 months
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 67-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by his wife for evaluation of a gradually progressive right hand tremor and generalized slowing over the past 18 months. He first became aware of an intermittent tremor in his right hand approximately 18 months ago, initially noticed while sitting quietly at home or during Zoom calls when he was not actively using his hands. The tremor was subtle at first and did not interfere with tasks, but over the subsequent year it became more frequent and prominent. His wife first drew his attention to it approximately 12 months ago when she noticed his right hand shaking on his lap during a family dinner. He reports that the tremor diminishes or temporarily stops when he uses his hand for purposeful tasks but reappears when he brings his arm back to rest.

Over the past year, Mr. Mehta has noticed increasing difficulty with tasks requiring fine motor coordination. Buttoning his dress shirts and formal kurtas has become laborious, particularly the smaller buttons, and he now enlists his wife's help. His handwriting, which he prided himself on for his calligraphy hobby, has become progressively smaller and more cramped — friends have commented that they can barely read his letters. He has abandoned calligraphy entirely in the past three months.

Both the patient and his wife have noticed changes in his walking over the past 12 months. He walks with less swing in his right arm and takes smaller, slower steps than before. He has had two episodes of near-falling when turning quickly, though no actual falls to the ground. He describes a sense of his feet feeling 'heavy' when initiating gait, particularly after sitting for an extended period. His wife notes that his voice has become noticeably softer and that his facial expression seems less animated than it used to be.

Of note, the patient and his wife report that his ability to smell common foods and household odors has been clearly diminished for the past two to three years. He no longer notices the scent of spices cooking or freshly brewed tea, something his wife specifically remarks upon. He initially attributed this to 'getting older.' He denies acting out dreams during sleep, though his wife has not observed any such behavior. He reports some constipation over the past year requiring a fiber supplement. He denies lightheadedness upon standing, hallucinations, cognitive complaints, difficulty swallowing, or urinary urgency beyond mild nocturia. He denies any exposure to antipsychotic medications, antiemetic dopamine blockers, or toxins. There is no history of encephalitis, significant head trauma, or family history of Parkinson's disease.

results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.summary: The MDS 2015 criteria define clinically established PD as parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity), absence of absolute exclusion criteria, two or more supportive criteria, and no red flags. Supportive criteria include clear dramatic response to dopaminergic therapy, rest tremor of a limb, olfactory loss, and levodopa-induced dyskinesia. The criteria require at least two supportive features for the highest level of diagnostic certainty.

results.title: Levodopa in Parkinson's Disease: PD MED Trial
results.authors: Gray R, Ives N, Rick C, et al.
results.summary: Levodopa-based therapy yielded superior patient-rated quality of life and motor benefit compared to initial treatment with dopamine agonists or MAO-B inhibitors in early Parkinson's disease. Levodopa is considered the most effective symptomatic therapy.

results.title: The New Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease
results.summary: Updated review of MDS criteria emphasizing the role of supportive features (hyposmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, cardiac sympathetic denervation) and the value of DaTscan in cases of clinical uncertainty. DaTscan abnormality in the context of parkinsonism supports a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit but does not distinguish PD from atypical parkinsonism.

output.summary: The MDS 2015 criteria for clinically established PD require parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity), at least two supportive criteria, no absolute exclusion criteria, and no red flags. Hyposmia (olfactory loss) is a well-validated supportive criterion present in approximately 90% of PD patients. Clear and dramatic beneficial response to dopaminergic therapy constitutes a separate supportive criterion. Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy for PD; PD MED trial data support early levodopa initiation, particularly when functional impairment is present. DaTscan demonstrates a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit and is useful when there is clinical uncertainty between PD and essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.

interactions: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction with amlodipine
No significant interaction with pantoprazole; pantoprazole does not impair levodopa absorption
contraindications: Non-selective MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine): risk of hypertensive crisis; patient must be free of non-selective MAO inhibitors for at least 2 weeks before initiating levodopa — none currently prescribed

Dopamine receptor antagonists (typical and atypical antipsychotics [e.g., haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine], antiemetics with D2-blocking activity [e.g., metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine]): pharmacologically antagonize levodopa and can worsen parkinsonism — none currently prescribed
warnings: Amlodipine and levodopa may have additive blood pressure-lowering effects; monitor for orthostatic hypotension after initiation, particularly in the morning

High-protein meals can competitively inhibit levodopa absorption at the intestinal level and at the blood-brain barrier; advise consistent protein distribution and taking levodopa 30-60 minutes before meals when possible
Iron-containing supplements and antacids (if prescribed) may reduce levodopa absorption; take levodopa 2 hours apart from iron

Selegiline (MAO-B inhibitor) in combination with levodopa is generally well tolerated but can rarely cause serotonergic interactions at high doses; if rasagiline or selegiline are considered adjuncts, avoid dietary tyramine excess
Monitor for dopamine dysregulation syndrome (impulse control disorders: pathological gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating); more common with dopamine agonists but can occur with levodopa
output.formulary_status: Generic carbidopa-levodopa on formulary; no prior authorization required
alternatives: Rasagiline 1 mg once daily (MAO-B inhibitor, mild symptomatic benefit, suitable for early disease with minimal functional impairment)
Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily, titrated gradually (dopamine agonist; higher risk of somnolence, impulse control disorders, orthostatic hypotension in elderly)
Ropinirole 0.25 mg three times daily, titrated gradually (dopamine agonist)
Rotigotine transdermal patch 2 mg/24 hours (dopamine agonist, once-daily patch)

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease: parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor and rigidity) with at least two supportive features (hyposmia and dramatic levodopa response), no absolute exclusion criteria, and no red flags
Document asymmetric onset with right-worse rest tremor at 4-6 Hz, re-emergent tremor on posture, cogwheel rigidity, and bradykinesia as satisfying the MDS motor core criteria

Review the full medication list for dopamine receptor antagonists (typical and atypical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine) and confirm no such agent is present before attributing parkinsonism to a neurodegenerative etiology

Confirm that the mild action/postural tremor component does not alter the diagnosis — rest tremor with re-emergence, bradykinesia, and asymmetric rigidity distinguish idiopathic PD from essential tremor
Initiate carbidopa-levodopa or a dopamine agonist as first-line therapy and document the levodopa response as an additional supportive criterion for the MDS diagnosis
Refer for physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology (LSVT-LOUD/BIG protocols)
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea in a patient with parkinsonism — these dopamine D2 receptor antagonists will worsen motor function

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) for behavioral symptoms — restrict PD psychosis pharmacotherapy to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin

Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a 67-year-old with even mild cognitive changes — high risk of delirium and cognitive decline in older adults with PD
key_reasoning_points: Asymmetric right-worse rest tremor (4-6 Hz) with re-emergence on posture, cogwheel rigidity, and bradykinesia satisfies the MDS 2015 motor criterion for parkinsonism; combined with hyposmia (supportive criterion 1) and a clear dramatic levodopa response (supportive criterion 2), this patient meets clinically established PD

The mild action/postural tremor component at 6-8 Hz is a red herring that may raise concern for essential tremor — however, essential tremor does not produce rest tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity; the co-presence of all three motor features conclusively favors PD

DaTscan shows markedly reduced LEFT putaminal dopamine transporter uptake, which is CONTRALATERAL to the clinically more affected RIGHT side — this laterality is anatomically correct and confirms the presynaptic nigrostriatal deficit
No dopamine receptor antagonists are present in the medication list, ruling out drug-induced parkinsonism as the primary diagnosis
Normal brain MRI excludes vascular parkinsonism, NPH, and structural causes; absent cerebellar signs, vertical gaze palsy, or early falls exclude atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP)

red_herrings.data_point: Mild action/postural tremor at 6-8 Hz observed when arms are extended on neurological exam, in addition to rest tremor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raise concern for essential tremor or a mixed tremor disorder rather than PD, especially given maternal family history of ET
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A mild postural/action tremor component can accompany idiopathic PD (re-emergent tremor has a latency distinguishing it from ET); the co-presence of bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, asymmetric rest tremor, and dramatic levodopa response conclusively identifies PD — essential tremor does not produce these features
